trends.name: AI adoption and labor displacement
trends.what_it_is: AI tools are automating routine cognitive and physical work across every sector—from accounting to medical diagnostics to creative services. Winners deploy AI fast and retain workers in higher-value roles; losers face talent exodus and margin collapse.

trends.who_wins: Firms that invest in AI for productivity and retrain workers for higher-value work stay profitable; firms that deploy it only to cut headcount face skill collapse.
trends.who_loses: Routine service providers (data entry, junior consulting, basic diagnostics) and firms that can't afford AI tooling lose pricing power and talent.

trends.name: Tariff-driven cost shock and supply chain upheaval
trends.what_it_is: Tariffs (25-54% on China imports, USMCA reciprocal duties) are raising input costs across manufacturing, retail, and trade. Companies are scrambling to nearshore to Mexico, Vietnam, or India while trying to pass costs through to consumers. Margins are getting squeezed.

trends.who_loses: Importers with thin margins (retail, food, components), companies unable to pass through costs, and small suppliers lacking negotiating power.

trends.name: Consolidation and scale-driven shakeout
trends.what_it_is: Across sectors, consolidation is accelerating. Larger, well-capitalized firms are buying or squeezing out independents and mid-market players. Small operators can't afford tech, can't absorb cost inflation, and face churn. Winners have scale; losers exit or get absorbed.

trends.name: Reimbursement pressure and pricing power collapse
trends.what_it_is: Across healthcare, Medicare cuts are eroding margins; insurance companies and hospital systems are squeezing suppliers and service providers. Wage inflation outpaces reimbursement growth, forcing closures and consolidation.

trends.who_wins: Large integrated healthcare systems and insurers with scale and data; companies bundling services and shifting to value-based care.
trends.who_loses: Solo practitioners, small medical practices, and independent clinics; specialists without volume; any provider reliant on a single payer.

trends.name: Labor shortage and wage spiral
trends.what_it_is: Across construction, healthcare, transportation, and hospitality, critical worker shortages are driving wages up 5-25% annually. Automation is a partial fix but raises capex barriers. Smaller operators can't compete on wages and exit.

trends.who_wins: High-wage operators and automation-ready firms that offer upskilling paths; companies bundling benefits and culture.
trends.who_loses: Low-wage hospitality, construction, and retail; small independent operators can't match wages; rural regions lose talent to urban centers.

trends.name: Energy demand surge from AI and data centers
trends.what_it_is: Data center buildout for AI is creating a structural surge in electricity demand, grid bottlenecks, and opportunities for power-adjacent industries. Companies with energy access thrive; those without face cost and availability headwinds.
industries: US Coal & Natural Gas Power Generation
US Data Processing and Hosting Services
trends.who_wins: Utilities, transmission operators, and power generators with scale and grid access; colocation and data-center operators in power-rich regions.
trends.who_loses: Energy-intensive manufacturing in power-scarce regions; small ISPs unable to attract server tenants; regions with grid constraints.

trends.name: Real estate bifurcation and office crisis
trends.what_it_is: Office real estate is in structural decline as hybrid work sticks. Data centers and logistics booming; multifamily under pressure from oversupply and affordability crisis. Residential and retail parcels shifting to conversion and adaptive reuse.
trends.who_wins: Developers investing in logistics, multifamily, and adaptive reuse; owners of prime office parcels in major metros converting to residential.
trends.who_loses: Legacy office landlords and tenants; retail real estate; suburban office parks; small commercial landlords.

trends.name: Channel shift: e-commerce and direct-to-consumer displacement of physical retail
trends.what_it_is: E-commerce and direct-to-consumer brands are pulling sales from physical retail, especially mid-market brick-and-mortar. Standalone stores are closing; survivors integrate omnichannel or go niche and experiential.

trends.name: Demographic dividend: aging population driving demand in healthcare and senior living
trends.what_it_is: Baby boomers are entering peak care years (65+). This is boosting demand for orthopedic procedures, hearing aids, senior housing, long-term care, and age-related treatments. Margins are under pressure but volume is strong.

trends.who_loses: Small independent practitioners and providers; companies serving younger demographics.

trends.name: Margin compression from inflation and input costs
trends.what_it_is: Across food, manufacturing, and retail, input costs (labor, materials, energy, tariffs) are rising faster than pricing power allows. Margins are shrinking; companies are cutting costs through automation and reducing choice.

trends.name: Consolidation and scale in media, publishing, and entertainment
trends.what_it_is: Streaming is consolidating into a few mega-platforms; content costs are rising; traditional media (cable, print) is declining. Consolidation is happening across music publishing, book houses, and ad agencies.

trends.who_loses: Traditional TV networks; ad-dependent publishers; mid-market creative shops; theater and live-event operators in weak markets.

trends.name: Health consciousness and dietary shift away from sugar and alcohol
trends.what_it_is: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, health awareness (especially among Gen Z), and regulatory scrutiny are cutting demand for sugary, alcoholic, and calorie-dense foods. Premiumization (organic, functional, low-alcohol) is rising but volumes are shrinking.

trends.who_wins: Functional and low-calorie food makers; premium spirits and wine; better-for-you snacks and beverages.
trends.who_loses: Traditional sugary food and beverage makers (soda, energy drinks, cheap spirits); mass-market ice cream and candy.

trends.name: Regulatory fragmentation and compliance cost explosion
trends.what_it_is: AI governance (SEC, FTC, NAIC), climate disclosure, cybersecurity (state-level), tariff rules, accessibility (ADA), and data privacy (GDPR, CPRA, CCPA) are creating a patchwork of regulations. Compliance costs are rising; smaller firms can't absorb them.

trends.who_wins: Large firms with dedicated compliance and legal teams; specialist consultants; consulting firms and law firms advising on regulation.
trends.who_loses: Small independent operators; mid-market firms without scale; single-jurisdiction service providers.

trends.name: Fintech and embedded finance disrupting traditional banking and payments
trends.what_it_is: Direct-to-consumer lending, embedded finance (payments in apps), BNPL, and stablecoins are bypassing traditional banking rails. Banks are consolidating and modernizing; small regional players are exiting.
industries: US Credit Card Processing & Money Transferring Industry
trends.who_wins: Large diversified banks; fintech platforms and embedded-finance providers; alternative-credit startups and marketplaces.
trends.who_loses: Regional and community banks; single-product banking services; traditional credit brokers.

trends.name: Premiumization and bifurcation: affluent vs. value consumers diverging
trends.what_it_is: Affluent consumers are spending on premium, experiential, and luxury goods; middle-class consumers are trading down to value/discount brands. Middle market is hollowed out. Niches (premium coffee, luxury fashion) thrive; mass-market mid-tier collapses.

trends.name: Supply chain shortages and geopolitical volatility
trends.what_it_is: Semiconductor shortages, shipping delays, geopolitical trade wars (US-China, US-EU), and climate disruptions (water scarcity, crop failures) are causing boom-bust cycles in supply. Companies are hedging via nearshoring and inventory building.

trends.who_wins: Nearshore manufacturers and companies with vertical integration; large players with hedging and inventory capacity.
trends.who_loses: Small suppliers dependent on single geographies; just-in-time manufacturers without buffers.

trends.name: Gig economy and fractional work blurring permanent employment
trends.what_it_is: Contractors, fractional roles, and gig platforms are normalizing across consulting, executive search, and creative services. Permanent employment is declining; benefits and stability are eroding. Workers are diversifying income sources.
trends.who_wins: Platforms connecting gig workers and fractional roles; consulting firms pivoting to advisory and interim placements; niche specialists.
trends.who_loses: Permanent corporate staffing models; job security in traditional roles; benefits-dependent workers.

trends.name: Alternative ownership: PE, REIT, and institutional capital reshaping industries
trends.what_it_is: Private equity is rolling up fragmented service industries (dental, health, fitness, restaurants). REITs are consolidating real estate. Sovereign wealth and institutional investors are buying real assets (catalogs, infrastructure, land). This favors scale and operational discipline but squeezes margins and cuts independent ownership.

trends.who_loses: Independent owner-operators; single-location businesses; small multi-unit operators without scale.

headline: Across 221 industries in 2025-2026, AI, tariffs, labor shortages, consolidation, and demographic aging are reshaping every sector—with scale leaders and automated players winning, small independents struggling to exit, and margins compressed nearly everywhere.
